To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ethanol and/or carbon-tetrachloride administration in rats induces the presence of IgG antibodies over the hepatocyte surface, which suggests that ethanol may be inducing hepatic injury mediated through IgG autoantigens which may be a reaction against an antigenic determinant present in hepatocyte membrane altered by ethanol and carbon-tetrachlroride treatment.
ethanol and/or carbon-tetrachloride administration to rats for 6 months, induces an increase in the IgG autoantigenicity of hepatocyte membranes.
ethanol induces hepatic injury mediated, at least in part, by IgG auto-antibodies, which may be a reaction to an antigenical alteration in hepatocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the demonstration that the hepatocellular damage produced by chronic ethanol consumption and/or carbon tatrachloride intoxication in the rat is accompanied by the presence of immunoglobulins (IgG) over the hepatocyte surface.
the presence of IgG in the hepatocytes' surfaces of ethanol- and/or CCl4-pretreated rats, which may be related to an antigenical alteration of hepatocytes induced by ethanol and CCl4.
the demonstration of the presence of IgG on hepatocyte's surface of ethanol- and/or CC14-treated rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ethanol, in addition to its direct cytotoxicity, may also induce hepatic injury by the production of IgG antibodies against an antigenical determinant of the hepatocyte membrane altered by ethanol and carbon tatrachloride.
the presence of IgG on the hepatocytes' membrane is a result of the ethanol and/or carbon tetra-chloride administration.
the IgG autoantigenic determinant is present in hepatocytes of normal rats but is not recognized by the immune system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of autoantibodies against hepatocyte membrane may be involved in ethanol-induced hepatic injury and that carbon tetrachlirde potentiates this effect.
ethanol may induce a chronic hepatic injury mediated, at least in part, by IgG auto-antibodies.
ethanol induces hepatic injury mediated in part by autoantibodies directed against altered hepatocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the IgG antibody in the diagnosis of alcoholic liver disease should be considered.
the use of a single dose of ethanol and/or carbon tetra-chloride in rats is not sufficient to produce hepatic injury mediated via IgG autoantigens.
the liver is a target organ for IgG autoantigens in ethanol- and CCl4-treated animals.
